verses.text: Moreover, brethren, I declare unto you the gospel which I preached unto you, which also ye have received, and wherein ye stand;
By which also ye are saved, if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain.
For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures;
And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures:
And that he was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve:
After that, he was seen of above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present, but some are fallen asleep.
After that, he was seen of James; then of all the apostles.
And last of all he was seen of me also, as of one born out of due time.
For I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.
But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.
Therefore whether it were I or they, so we preach, and so ye believed.
Now if Christ be preached that he rose from the dead, how say some among you that there is no resurrection of the dead?
But if there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen:
And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain.
Yea, and we are found false witnesses of God; because we have testified of God that he raised up Christ: whom he raised not up, if so be that the dead rise not.
For if the dead rise not, then is not Christ raised:
And if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain; ye are yet in your sins.
Then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished.
If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable.
But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.
For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead.
For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.
But every man in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming.
Then cometh the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father; when he shall have put down all rule and all authority and power.
For he must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet.
The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death.
For he hath put all things under his feet. But when he saith all things are put under him, it is manifest that he is excepted, which did put all things under him.
And when all things shall be subdued unto him, then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him that put all things under him, that God may be all in all.
Else what shall they do which are baptized for the dead, if the dead rise not at all? why are they then baptized for the dead?
And why stand we in jeopardy every hour?
I protest by your rejoicing which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die daily.
If after the manner of men I have fought with beasts at Ephesus, what advantageth it me, if the dead rise not? let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die.
Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.
Awake to righteousness, and sin not; for some have not the knowledge of God: I speak this to your shame.
But some man will say, How are the dead raised up? and with what body do they come?
Thou fool, that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die:
And that which thou sowest, thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain, it may chance of wheat, or of some other grain:
But God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him, and to every seed his own body.
All flesh is not the same flesh: but there is one kind of flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds.
There are also celestial bodies, and bodies terrestrial: but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another.
There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differeth from another star in glory.
So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption:
It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power:
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.
And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit.
Howbeit that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural; and afterward that which is spiritual.
The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven.
As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy: and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly.
And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.
Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption.
Behold, I shew you a mystery; We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,
In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.
For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.
So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.
O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?
The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law.
But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.

summary: Paul turns from disorder in the assembly to the foundation underneath everything he has argued, reminding the Corinthians of “the gospel which I preached unto you, which also ye have received, and wherein ye stand,” by which they are saved “if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain.” What he hands on he first received: “how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures.” Then the witnesses are counted out one after another — “seen of Cephas, then of the twelve,” “of above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present,” “of James; then of all the apostles,” and “last of all he was seen of me also, as of one born out of due time,” by a man who calls himself “the least of the apostles” because “I persecuted the church of God,” yet who can say “by the grace of God I am what I am.” Only then does the problem surface: “how say some among you that there is no resurrection of the dead?” Paul runs that denial to its end without softening it. “If there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen”; preaching is vain and faith is vain; the apostles are “found false witnesses of God”; “ye are yet in your sins”; those “fallen asleep in Christ are perished”; and “if in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable.” Against that ruin he sets one sentence: “But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.” Two men are set head to head — “for as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive” — and an order is laid out: “Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming,” then “the end,” when the kingdom is delivered up and “all rule and all authority and power” put down, for “he must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet,” and “the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death,” until at last “God may be all in all.” Practical arguments follow in quick succession: the much-disputed “what shall they do which are baptized for the dead, if the dead rise not at all?”; Paul’s own exposure, “why stand we in jeopardy every hour?” and “I die daily”; his fight “with beasts at Ephesus”; and the only honest alternative if the grave is final, “let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die.” He breaks off into warning — “evil communications corrupt good manners” — and summons: “Awake to righteousness, and sin not; for some have not the knowledge of God: I speak this to your shame.” To the sceptic’s question, “How are the dead raised up? and with what body do they come?”, he answers with seed and starlight. What is sown “is not quickened, except it die,” and “thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain,” while “God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him, and to every seed his own body.” As “one star differeth from another star in glory,” so the risen body differs from the buried one: “it is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body.” The two Adams frame the whole — “the first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit,” “the first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven” — and the promise is that “as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.” The chapter ends in mystery and trumpet. “Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption,” yet “we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump,” when “this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality,” and the old word comes true: “Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?” Because “the sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law,” the thanks belong wholly to God “which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” — and the argument lands, characteristically, as a command to keep working: “be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.”
takeaways: Paul introduces the resurrection not as his insight but as a delivery: “I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received.” He presents himself as a link in a chain rather than an origin, and the content he passes on is already fixed and confessional in shape — died for our sins, was buried, rose the third day, was seen. That handing-on is what makes the gospel checkable: he can name Cephas, the twelve, James, “above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present,” effectively inviting anyone who doubts to go and ask them. And it is not merely informational, since salvation is bound to holding it fast: they are saved “if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain.”

The chain of consequences in verses 13-19 refuses to let the resurrection be an optional appendix to Christian faith. If the dead are not raised, then Christ is not raised; if Christ is not raised, “then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain”; worse, the apostles are “found false witnesses of God,” not merely mistaken but slanderers of him. Most striking is what Paul says collapses next: “ye are yet in your sins.” Forgiveness is not something the cross secures independently of Easter and to which the resurrection merely adds confirmation. And the honest conclusion, if it were all untrue, is not a diminished but still admirable religion — it is that “we are of all men most miserable.”

“Firstfruits” is a harvest word, and Paul leans on everything it implies: “now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.” The first sheaf is not a different crop from the rest but the same crop arriving early, so Christ’s risen body is a specimen of what is promised rather than a unique exception to the rule of death. From this comes both a sequence — “Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming” — and a destination, since “the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death” and the reign of the Son ends not in his own aggrandizement but “that God may be all in all.” Christian hope here is not escape from embodiment but the abolition of the thing that ends embodied life.

Asked “with what body do they come?” Paul neither retreats into a bodiless afterlife nor promises a mere resuscitation of the corpse. The seed answers both errors at once: “that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die,” and “thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain.” There is real continuity — the same seed, “to every seed his own body” — and real transformation, hammered out in four matched pairs: “sown in corruption... raised in incorruption... sown in dishonour... raised in glory... sown in weakness... raised in power... sown a natural body... raised a spiritual body.” The “spiritual body” is not a body made of spirit but a body wholly answerable to the Spirit, which is why “flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God” denies the survival of mortality, not of matter.

The chapter’s anthropology is corporate before it is individual. Every human being is described as wearing a likeness received from another: “the first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit,” and “as is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy: and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly.” Death is therefore not a private biological fact but an inheritance — “since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead” — and glory is likewise received rather than achieved: “as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.” Solidarity with Adam is unchosen; solidarity with Christ is offered.

The most abstract chapter Paul ever wrote ends with a work order. “Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.” The word “vain” has been the chapter’s refrain — preaching vain, faith vain, believing in vain — and it is now decisively negated on the other side. If the body has a future, then what is done in the body is not wasted motion, and the contrary slogan Paul quoted, “let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die,” is exposed as the only rational ethic for people with no resurrection. Doctrine here is not the opposite of practicality; it is what makes endurance reasonable.

crossRefs.label: Romans 5:12-21 — as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin
crossRefs.why: Paul works out at length there the head-to-head comparison he states in compressed form here, “for as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.” Reading the two together shows that the resurrection argument rests on a doctrine of representation: death spread through one man’s act, and life is conveyed the same way, which is why Christ’s rising is not an isolated marvel but the beginning of a race’s reversal.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 25:8 — He will swallow up death in victory
crossRefs.why: Paul’s climactic “then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory” quotes this promise directly. In its own setting it belongs to a feast on the mountain for all peoples, where God wipes away tears from every face, so Paul is claiming that the general resurrection is the fulfilment of a hope Israel already held rather than a new idea imported into the faith.

crossRefs.label: Hosea 13:14 — O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction
crossRefs.why: The taunt Paul raises over the emptied grave, “O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?”, is drawn from this oracle of ransom from the power of the grave. Set beside the prophet’s words, Paul’s question is not a rhetorical flourish but the mockery of a defeated enemy whose destruction God had already announced.

crossRefs.label: Daniel 12:2-3 — many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake... shall shine as the brightness of the firmament
crossRefs.why: Two of this chapter’s central images are already joined here: sleep as the figure for death, which Paul uses of those “fallen asleep in Christ,” and astral glory for the risen righteous, which stands behind “one star differeth from another star in glory.” The prophecy also holds together resurrection and judgment, which is the framework within which Paul places the delivering up of the kingdom.

crossRefs.label: Philippians 3:21 — Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body
crossRefs.why: This states in one line what the seed analogy argues at length, that the same body is changed rather than discarded, and it identifies the pattern of the change as Christ’s own risen body. It confirms that “we shall also bear the image of the heavenly” means conformity to a particular person and not absorption into a general spiritual condition.

crossRefs.label: 2 Maccabees 12:43-45 — in that he was mindful of the resurrection... it had been superfluous and vain to pray for the dead
crossRefs.why: This passage joins the same two convictions Paul joins in the puzzling verse about those “baptized for the dead”: that the dead will rise, and that the living may act religiously on their behalf. Whatever the Corinthian practice was, the pairing was not unheard of in the Jewish world Paul came from, and this text is where the Catholic tradition finds the clearest scriptural precedent for it.

interpretationNotes.claim: On “Else what shall they do which are baptized for the dead, if the dead rise not at all? why are they then baptized for the dead?”, the Catholic reading grants that Paul neither describes the practice nor commends it, and the tradition has never taught a vicarious sacrament administered to the living on behalf of the departed. What it does take from the verse is the underlying assumption Paul finds unremarkable enough to argue from: that there is a real bond between the living Church and the dead, and that what the living do can bear on the state of those who have died. That conviction is what the communion of saints names, and it is why prayer, almsgiving, and above all the offering of the Eucharist for the departed are regarded as ancient and coherent rather than as later accretions. The argument only works, Paul says, because the dead rise; the same logic supports intercession for them, since one does not pray for those with no future.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters emphasize Paul’s grammar: he says “they” and not “we,” shifting to the first person only in the next breath with “why stand we in jeopardy every hour?” On the common reading this is an argument from an opponent’s inconsistency — some in Corinth were doing something that presupposed a future for the dead while others denied that future — and Paul exploits the contradiction without approving the rite. More broadly, Protestant theology holds that each person is judged on the basis of Christ’s finished work received by faith in this life, so no sacrament and no prayer can transfer benefit across death, and a verse this obscure cannot establish a practice the rest of Scripture never commands. Both traditions agree on what the verse assumes and what it is used to prove: that the resurrection of the dead is real, and that any practice premised on the dead having no future is incoherent for a Christian.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition reads the chapter’s account of glory as graded and as requiring a real fitness in the one glorified. “There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differeth from another star in glory” is taken to describe not only the difference between earthly and heavenly bodies but genuine degrees of beatitude among the saved, corresponding to the charity in which each died — which is why the chapter can close by insisting that “your labour is not in vain in the Lord.” Alongside this, “flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption” is read as stating an absolute condition: nothing corruptible passes into glory. Since many die genuinely in grace yet still attached to sin and unfree of its residue, the tradition concludes that a final purification completes what grace began, so that the incorruption Paul describes is not a legal exemption from holiness but its actual attainment.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings answer that Paul locates the whole change in a single divine act at the end: “we shall all be changed, In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump.” An instantaneous transformation wrought by God at the trumpet leaves no room and no need for an intervening process undergone by the soul, and the chapter never hints at one. The heavenly bodies in verses 40-41 are ordinarily read as an argument about God’s freedom in fitting bodies to their spheres — he “giveth it a body as it hath pleased him” — rather than as a taxonomy of rewards, and “flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God” is read as a statement about mortality, not about unpurged guilt. The believer’s title to glory is Christ’s righteousness received by faith, and glorification is God’s immediate completion of that gift. Both traditions affirm that nothing unfit enters the kingdom, that the fitting is God’s work and not the creature’s achievement, and that what is raised is transformed rather than merely revived.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes seriously the conditional Paul attaches to salvation in the opening lines: they are saved by the gospel “if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain.” Faith is presented as something that can be held and also let go, and believing itself can turn out to have been in vain, which supports the tradition’s teaching that justification once received can be lost through grave sin or apostasy and that perseverance is a gift to be prayed for rather than a possession already secured. The chapter’s last verse is read in the same key: the exhortation to be “stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord” is given a motive — “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” — so that works done in grace genuinely count toward the glory that follows rather than merely evidencing a verdict already fixed.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters divide here, though less sharply than the caricature suggests. Those holding that the elect necessarily persevere read “unless ye have believed in vain” as describing faith that was never genuine, an empty profession exposed by its failure to hold, and they point out that Paul’s very next move is to attribute everything he is and does to grace — “by the grace of God I am what I am” — which is also how perseverance itself is supplied. Those holding that a real believer may fall away read the conditional much as the Catholic tradition does, while still denying that continuance is a work the believer contributes. On the closing verse, Protestant readings generally take “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” as a promise of God’s gracious reward for work he himself enables, not as merit strictly owed. Both traditions agree that the warning is meant to be heard as a warning, that a faith which does not endure does not save, and that whatever endurance the Christian has is grace at work.

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.
